about: A112/Atlas · DRAFTED DEFINITIONS for the Atlas's non-computing skills and tools, written by the agent in its own words (no source copied) for the OWNER'S REVIEW. Seeded at boot into atlas_nodes.definition_draft ONLY (definition_by = 'drafted') — never into `definition` — so nothing public shows them and the auto-publish bar does not count them until the owner accepts them in Admin → Atlas → Drafted definitions (D105 P11). A node that already has a definition or a waiting draft, or whose draft the owner rejected, is never touched; a slug with no node is skipped. Same rules as the chat import: one or two sentences, 20–400 characters, no links. Grouped by family; batch 1 (11-03): sales, finance & FP&A, accounting & audit, the three marketing families, product, workplace tools.

sales.salesforce: A customer relationship management platform where sales teams record accounts, contacts, opportunities and forecasts. Sellers use it to track every deal from first contact to close and managers use it to report on the pipeline.
sales.prospecting: Finding and researching potential customers who fit the company's target profile, then making first contact with them. It fills the top of the sales pipeline with new opportunities.
sales.consultative-selling: A sales approach in which the seller asks questions to understand a buyer's situation and problems before recommending a solution. The seller acts as an adviser rather than pushing a fixed product.
sales.sales-targets: The revenue, deal-count or activity goals a seller or team is expected to reach in a period. Pay and performance reviews in sales roles are usually tied to them.
sales.cold-calling: Telephoning prospective customers who have had no earlier contact with the company to introduce a product and book a conversation. It is a core activity in early-career sales development roles.
sales.outside-sales: Selling in person by visiting customers at their offices or sites, usually across an assigned territory. It contrasts with inside sales, which is done remotely.
sales.zoominfo: A business contact and company database that sales and marketing teams use to find prospects, phone numbers, emails and firmographic details. It is often connected to the CRM to enrich account records.
sales.product-demonstrations: Showing a prospective customer how a product works, live or recorded, focused on the problems that buyer cares about. A demo usually follows discovery and moves a deal toward evaluation.
sales.territory-management: Planning how a seller covers an assigned set of accounts or a region: which customers to prioritise, how often to contact them and how to grow revenue there.
sales.solution-selling: A sales method that starts from the customer's business problem and positions the product as the answer to it, rather than leading with features.
sales.closing-experience: A track record of taking sales opportunities through negotiation to a signed contract. Postings ask for it to show the seller has personally won deals, not only generated leads.
sales.closing-deals: Bringing a sales opportunity to a signed agreement by handling final objections, agreeing terms and securing the buyer's commitment.
sales.meddpicc: A sales qualification framework that checks a deal for metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, paper process, identified pain, a champion and the competition. Teams use it to judge which deals are real and what is missing.
sales.cross-selling: Offering an existing customer additional products that complement what they already buy. It grows revenue from accounts the company already has.
sales.value-selling: Selling by quantifying the business value a customer will get, such as money saved or revenue gained, and anchoring the conversation and price on that value.
sales.new-business-development: Winning customers the company has never sold to before, as opposed to growing existing accounts. Roles focused on it are often called hunter roles.
sales.sales-methodology: A defined, repeatable way a sales team runs deals, such as a qualification framework or a selling approach that everyone on the team follows. It makes forecasting and coaching consistent.
sales.sales-calls: Phone or video conversations with prospects or customers to qualify, present, negotiate or follow up on a deal.
sales.quota-attainment: How much of an assigned sales quota a seller actually achieved, expressed as a percentage. Postings ask for a history of meeting or exceeding quota as evidence of performance.
sales.product-demos: Live or recorded walkthroughs of a product for a prospective customer, tailored to the problems that buyer described. A demo usually follows discovery in the sales process.
sales.inside-sales: Selling remotely by phone, email and video rather than in person. Inside sales teams often handle higher volumes of smaller or mid-sized deals.
sales.full-cycle-sales: Owning a deal from first prospecting through discovery, demo, negotiation and close, instead of handing it between specialised roles.
sales.clari: A revenue platform that pulls activity and deal data from the CRM, email and calendar to forecast sales and flag deals at risk.
sales.upselling: Persuading an existing customer to buy a higher tier, more seats or a larger version of what they already use.
sales.sales-forecasting: Predicting how much revenue the team will close in a period, based on the pipeline, each deal's stage and past win rates.
sales.president-s-club: An award many companies give their top-performing sellers each year, often with a trip. Postings mention it as a sign of a candidate's past sales results.
sales.discovery-calls: Early conversations with a prospect to learn their situation, problems, goals, budget and buying process before proposing anything.
sales.lead-qualification: Deciding whether a potential customer is worth pursuing by checking fit, need, budget, authority and timing. Qualified leads are passed on to account executives.
sales.mutual-action-plans: A shared document a seller and buyer agree on that lists the steps, owners and dates needed to reach a decision. It keeps complex deals on schedule.
sales.meddic: A sales qualification framework that checks a deal for metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, identified pain and a champion. It helps sellers forecast accurately and focus on winnable deals.
sales.challenger-sale: A selling approach in which the seller teaches the customer something new about their business, tailors the message and takes control of the conversation, rather than simply building rapport.
sales.salesloft: A sales engagement platform that schedules and tracks sequences of emails, calls and tasks for sellers and records how prospects respond.
sales.linkedin-sales-navigator: LinkedIn's paid tool for sellers to search for prospects by company and role, save leads and follow account activity.
sales.seismic: A sales enablement platform that stores and recommends marketing content, decks and documents for sellers to share with buyers.
sales.cold-outreach: Contacting prospects who have had no earlier contact with the company, by email, phone or social messages, to start a sales conversation.
sales.spin-selling: A questioning method for sales conversations built on four question types: situation, problem, implication and need-payoff. It helps the buyer see the cost of their problem and the value of solving it.
sales.highspot: A sales enablement platform that organises content, playbooks and training for sellers and tracks how buyers engage with shared material.
sales.booked-meetings: Meetings a sales development representative schedules between a qualified prospect and an account executive. It is a common performance measure for those roles.
sales.pipedrive: A customer relationship management tool built around a visual sales pipeline, used mostly by smaller sales teams to track deals by stage.

fpa.forecasting: Estimating future results such as revenue, costs, demand or cash from past data, current trends and assumptions. Finance and operations teams update forecasts regularly to guide decisions.
fpa.treasury: The finance function that manages a company's cash, liquidity, bank relationships, borrowing, investments and currency or interest-rate risk.
fpa.portfolio-management: Choosing and managing a set of investments to meet return and risk goals, including deciding what to buy, hold or sell and rebalancing over time.
fpa.capital-markets: The markets where companies and governments raise money by issuing stocks and bonds, and where those securities are traded. Roles in this area structure, price, sell or trade such offerings.
fpa.financial-models: Spreadsheet models that project a business's revenue, costs, cash flow or value from a set of assumptions. They are used for planning, valuation and decisions such as investments or pricing.
fpa.p-l: The profit and loss statement, which reports a business's revenue, costs and resulting profit over a period. Roles that own a P&L are accountable for that unit's financial results.
fpa.valuation: Estimating what a company, asset or security is worth, using methods such as discounted cash flow, comparable companies and past transactions.
fpa.cfa: The Chartered Financial Analyst designation, a professional credential in investment analysis and portfolio management earned by passing three exams and meeting work-experience requirements.
fpa.management-reporting: Regular internal reports on financial and operating performance prepared for leaders, comparing results with budget and forecast and explaining the differences.
fpa.corporate-finance: The work of deciding how a company funds itself and invests its money, including capital structure, budgeting for investments, mergers and acquisitions and returning cash to shareholders.
fpa.variance-analysis: Comparing actual results with the budget or forecast and explaining why they differ, line by line.
fpa.bloomberg: The Bloomberg Terminal, a subscription system that delivers real-time market data, news, analytics and trading tools to finance professionals.
fpa.unit-economics: The revenue and costs tied to a single unit of a business, such as one customer or one order. It shows whether each unit is profitable and how that changes as the business grows.
fpa.scenario-analysis: Modelling how results would change under different sets of assumptions, such as a base, upside and downside case, to plan for uncertainty.
fpa.long-range-plan: A company's multi-year financial plan, usually three to five years, setting out expected growth, investments and profitability.
fpa.opex: Operating expenses: the ongoing costs of running a business, such as salaries, rent and software, as opposed to long-term capital investment.
fpa.annual-operating-plan: A company's budget and goals for the coming year, agreed by leadership, against which actual results are tracked.
fpa.credit-analysis: Judging how likely a borrower is to repay debt, by studying its financial statements, cash flows, collateral and industry risk.
fpa.working-capital: The money a business has tied up in its day-to-day operations, measured as current assets such as cash, receivables and inventory minus current liabilities such as payables.
fpa.hyperion: Oracle Hyperion, a family of enterprise performance-management software used for budgeting, forecasting, consolidation and financial reporting.
fpa.anaplan: A cloud planning platform used to build connected models for budgeting, forecasting, sales planning and workforce planning.
fpa.monthly-forecast: A forecast of revenue, costs or cash that finance updates each month with the latest results and assumptions.
fpa.budgeting-and-forecasting: Setting a financial plan for a period and then regularly re-estimating expected results as the period unfolds.
fpa.sensitivity-analysis: Testing how much a model's output changes when one input is changed at a time. It shows which assumptions matter most.
fpa.factset: A financial data and analytics platform that provides company financials, market data, estimates and screening tools to investment professionals.
fpa.equity-research: Analysing public companies and their shares to publish recommendations and price targets for investors, based on financial models and industry study.
fpa.capex: Capital expenditure: money spent on long-lived assets such as buildings, equipment or capitalised software, recorded on the balance sheet and depreciated over time.
fpa.board-reporting: Preparing the financial and operating materials presented to a company's board of directors, usually each quarter.
fpa.rolling-forecast: A forecast that always looks the same distance ahead, such as the next twelve months, adding a new period as each one closes.
fpa.dcf: Discounted cash flow, a valuation method that estimates what an asset is worth today by projecting its future cash flows and discounting them back by a required rate of return.
fpa.p-l-management: Being accountable for a business unit's revenue, costs and profit, including the decisions that move them.
fpa.capital-iq: S&P Capital IQ, a financial data platform with company financials, transaction records, ownership data and screening tools used in investment banking and research.
fpa.financial-modelling: Building spreadsheet models that project a business's revenue, costs, cash flow or value from a set of assumptions, to support planning, valuation and deals.
fpa.headcount-forecasting: Projecting how many people a company or team will employ over the planning period and what they will cost.
fpa.pitchbook: A data platform covering private companies, venture capital, private equity and mergers and acquisitions, used for deal sourcing and market research.
fpa.precedent-transactions: A valuation method that estimates a company's worth from the prices paid in past acquisitions of similar companies.
fpa.cash-flow-forecasting: Projecting the cash a business will receive and pay out over coming weeks or months, to make sure it can meet its obligations.
fpa.lbo: A leveraged buyout, the acquisition of a company funded largely with borrowed money, where the debt is repaid from the company's own cash flows.
fpa.cash-flow-analysis: Studying where a business's cash comes from and where it goes, across operating, investing and financing activities.
fpa.npv: Net present value: the value today of an investment's future cash flows, discounted at a required rate of return, minus its cost. A positive figure means the investment is expected to add value.
fpa.irr: Internal rate of return: the discount rate at which an investment's net present value is zero. It is used to compare the expected return of projects or deals.
fpa.adaptive-insights: Workday Adaptive Planning, a cloud tool for budgeting, forecasting and financial reporting.
fpa.essbase: Oracle Essbase, a multidimensional database used to store and analyse financial data for planning and reporting.
fpa.driver-based-models: Financial models in which results are calculated from a small number of operational drivers, such as headcount, price or volume, rather than entered line by line.
fpa.three-statement-model: A financial model that links the income statement, balance sheet and cash-flow statement so that a change to one assumption flows through all three.
fpa.refinitiv: A provider of financial market data, news and analytics, now part of the London Stock Exchange Group, used by traders and analysts.
fpa.comparable-company-analysis: A valuation method that estimates a company's worth from the trading multiples, such as price to earnings, of similar public companies.
fpa.planful: A cloud platform for financial planning, budgeting, consolidation and reporting.
fpa.budget-forecasting: Estimating future revenue and spending to set a budget, and re-estimating it as actual results come in.
fpa.driver-based-forecasting: Forecasting financial results from the operational drivers behind them, such as units sold, price or headcount.
fpa.budget-to-actual: A comparison of actual results with the budget for the same period, used to explain gaps and adjust plans.
fpa.capital-budgeting: Deciding which long-term investments, such as new equipment or projects, a company should fund, by comparing their expected returns and costs.
fpa.vena: A planning and budgeting platform built on Excel that adds a shared database, workflow and reporting for finance teams.

accounting_audit.payroll: Calculating and paying employees' wages, withholding taxes and deductions, and filing the related tax reports on time.
accounting_audit.cpa: Certified Public Accountant, a licensed accounting credential in the United States earned by passing the CPA exam and meeting education and experience requirements.
accounting_audit.financial-reporting: Preparing a company's financial statements and related reports for leaders, investors, lenders or regulators, following accounting standards.
accounting_audit.netsuite: Oracle NetSuite, a cloud ERP system that runs a company's general ledger, billing, purchasing, inventory and financial reporting.
accounting_audit.gaap: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles, the standard rules companies follow when preparing financial statements. In the United States they are set by the Financial Accounting Standards Board.
accounting_audit.external-audit: An independent examination of a company's financial statements by an outside accounting firm, which gives an opinion on whether they are fairly presented.
accounting_audit.accruals: Accounting entries that record revenue when it is earned and expenses when they are incurred, even if cash has not yet changed hands.
accounting_audit.journal-entries: Records in the general ledger that post a transaction as equal debits and credits to the affected accounts.
accounting_audit.accounts-payable: The money a company owes its suppliers, and the team and process that check, approve and pay those invoices.
accounting_audit.accounts-receivable: The money customers owe a company for goods or services already delivered, and the process of invoicing and collecting it.
accounting_audit.sox-controls: Internal controls over financial reporting that public companies must design, document and test under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.
accounting_audit.account-reconciliations: Checking that the balance of a general-ledger account matches supporting records, such as bank statements or subledgers, and explaining any difference.
accounting_audit.intercompany: Transactions between entities of the same group, such as a parent and its subsidiaries, which must be recorded on both sides and eliminated when the group's accounts are consolidated.
accounting_audit.revenue-accounting: Recording when and how much revenue a company recognises from its contracts, following standards such as ASC 606.
accounting_audit.close-process: The steps accounting completes at the end of each month, quarter or year to finalise the books, including reconciliations, accruals and review.
accounting_audit.us-gaap: The generally accepted accounting principles used in the United States, set by the Financial Accounting Standards Board.
accounting_audit.asc-606: The US accounting standard for revenue from contracts with customers. It sets out five steps for deciding when and how much revenue to recognise.
accounting_audit.tax-returns: The forms individuals and businesses file with tax authorities to report income and calculate the tax they owe.
accounting_audit.balance-sheet-reconciliations: Checking each balance-sheet account against supporting detail at period end and explaining or correcting any differences.
accounting_audit.indirect-tax: Taxes charged on transactions rather than on income, such as sales tax, VAT and GST, which businesses collect and pay to tax authorities.
accounting_audit.tax-provision: The calculation of a company's income-tax expense and the related current and deferred tax balances for its financial statements.
accounting_audit.vat: Value-added tax, a consumption tax charged at each stage of production and sale, which businesses collect and pass on to the tax authority.
accounting_audit.audit-support: Helping auditors by preparing schedules, documents and explanations they request during an audit.
accounting_audit.fixed-assets: Long-lived assets such as buildings, machinery and equipment, recorded on the balance sheet and depreciated over their useful lives.
accounting_audit.prepaids: Expenses paid in advance, such as insurance or software subscriptions, recorded as assets and expensed over the period they cover.
accounting_audit.gst: Goods and services tax, a value-added tax used in countries such as Canada, Australia and India.
accounting_audit.ifrs: International Financial Reporting Standards, the accounting standards issued by the IASB and used in most countries outside the United States.
accounting_audit.workiva: A cloud platform for preparing and filing financial reports, SEC filings and compliance documents, with linked data and review workflows.
accounting_audit.sales-and-use-tax: US state and local taxes on sales of goods and some services; use tax applies when sales tax was not charged at the time of purchase.
accounting_audit.pbc: Provided by client: the list of schedules and documents a company prepares and hands to its auditors.
accounting_audit.lease-accounting: Recording leases on the financial statements, including the right-of-use asset and lease liability required by ASC 842 and IFRS 16.
accounting_audit.blackline: A cloud platform that automates parts of the accounting close, including account reconciliations, journal entries and task tracking.
accounting_audit.avalara: Software that calculates, collects and files sales tax, VAT and other transaction taxes for businesses.
accounting_audit.oracle-financials: Oracle's financial software for the general ledger, payables, receivables and reporting, part of its ERP suites.
accounting_audit.audit-workpapers: The documents auditors prepare to record the procedures they performed, the evidence gathered and their conclusions.
accounting_audit.cost-accounting: Tracking and analysing what it costs to make a product or deliver a service, to support pricing, budgeting and cost control.
accounting_audit.quickbooks: Intuit's accounting software, widely used by small and mid-sized businesses for bookkeeping, invoicing and payroll.
accounting_audit.asc-842: The US accounting standard for leases. It requires most leases to appear on the balance sheet as a right-of-use asset and a lease liability.
accounting_audit.bank-reconciliations: Matching a company's cash records against its bank statements and explaining any differences.
accounting_audit.accounting-close: Finalising the accounting records at the end of a period so financial statements can be produced.
accounting_audit.sox-testing: Testing whether a company's internal controls over financial reporting are designed well and working, as the Sarbanes-Oxley Act requires.
accounting_audit.auditboard: A cloud platform for internal audit, SOX compliance and risk management work.
accounting_audit.sap-fico: The finance and controlling modules of SAP's ERP, covering the general ledger, payables, receivables, asset accounting and cost accounting.
accounting_audit.audit-fieldwork: The stage of an audit when the team gathers evidence, tests transactions and controls, and documents findings.
accounting_audit.sage-intacct: A cloud accounting and financial-management system used by mid-sized businesses.
accounting_audit.floqast: Close-management software that helps accounting teams organise month-end tasks and reconciliations.
accounting_audit.caseware: Software that auditors and accountants use to prepare working papers and financial statements.

marketing_brand.go-to-market: The plan for bringing a product to market: which customers to target, how to position and price it, and which channels and teams will sell it.
marketing_brand.product-marketing: The marketing function that positions a product, defines its messaging and target buyers, supports launches and equips sales to sell it.
marketing_brand.brand-strategy: A long-term plan for how a company wants to be perceived, covering its positioning, personality, promise and the way it differs from competitors.
marketing_brand.brand-awareness: How familiar a target audience is with a brand, and the marketing work aimed at increasing that familiarity.
marketing_brand.brand-management: Looking after how a brand is presented and perceived over time, keeping its positioning, identity and messages consistent.
marketing_brand.market-segmentation: Dividing a market into groups of customers with shared needs or traits, so products and messages can be targeted at each.

marketing_content.social-media: Using platforms such as LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok and X to publish content, engage an audience and promote a brand or product.
marketing_content.content-strategy: Planning what content an organisation creates, for which audience and purpose, and how it is produced, published and measured.
marketing_content.content-marketing: Attracting and keeping customers by publishing useful material, such as articles, guides, videos and newsletters, rather than direct advertising.
marketing_content.email-marketing: Sending marketing messages to a list of subscribers or customers by email, from newsletters to automated sequences, and measuring opens, clicks and conversions.
marketing_content.mailchimp: An email marketing platform for building subscriber lists, designing campaigns, automating sequences and reporting on results.
marketing_content.klaviyo: An email and SMS marketing platform, popular with e-commerce brands, for automated flows and segmented campaigns.
marketing_content.influencer-marketing: Working with creators who have engaged audiences on social media to promote a brand or product.
marketing_content.lifecycle-campaigns: Marketing messages timed to a customer's stage, from onboarding to renewal or win-back, to keep them engaged and buying.
marketing_content.sprout-social: A social media management platform for scheduling posts, managing messages, listening and reporting across networks.
marketing_content.hootsuite: A social media management tool for scheduling posts, monitoring mentions and reporting across several networks.
marketing_content.email-flows: Automated sequences of emails triggered by a customer's behaviour, such as signing up, abandoning a cart or making a purchase.

marketing_digital.pipeline-generation: Creating new qualified sales opportunities through marketing and outreach, measured by the value of pipeline sourced.
marketing_digital.demand-generation: Marketing aimed at creating interest in a product and turning it into qualified leads and sales pipeline, across campaigns, content and channels.
marketing_digital.paid-media: Advertising a company pays for, such as search ads, social ads, display and video, as opposed to earned or owned media.
marketing_digital.paid-social: Paid advertising on social platforms such as Meta, LinkedIn and TikTok, targeted to chosen audiences.
marketing_digital.customer-acquisition: Winning new customers through marketing and sales, usually measured by cost per acquisition and volume.
marketing_digital.campaign-management: Planning, launching, monitoring and optimising marketing campaigns across channels within a budget and timeline.
marketing_digital.seo: Search engine optimisation: improving a website's content, structure and links so it ranks higher in unpaid search results.
marketing_digital.abm: Account-based marketing, which targets a defined list of high-value accounts with personalised campaigns, working closely with sales.
marketing_digital.marketing-analytics: Measuring and analysing marketing performance, such as traffic, conversions, cost and return by channel, to guide spending and campaigns.
marketing_digital.ltv: Lifetime value: the total revenue or profit a business expects from a customer over the whole relationship.
marketing_digital.google-ads: Google's advertising platform for search, display, shopping and YouTube ads, bought by auction on keywords and audiences.
marketing_digital.marketo: Adobe Marketo Engage, a marketing automation platform for email campaigns, lead scoring and nurturing, usually in business-to-business marketing.
marketing_digital.hubspot: A CRM and marketing platform for email, landing pages, lead management, sales pipelines and customer service.
marketing_digital.linkedin-ads: LinkedIn's advertising platform, used mainly for business-to-business targeting by job title, company and industry.
marketing_digital.google-analytics: Google's web analytics service, which tracks website and app traffic, user behaviour and conversions.
marketing_digital.keyword-research: Finding the search terms people use for a topic and judging their volume and competition, to guide SEO content and paid search.
marketing_digital.meta-ads: Advertising on Facebook, Instagram and Meta's other apps, bought through Meta's Ads Manager.
marketing_digital.cac: Customer acquisition cost: the total sales and marketing spend divided by the number of new customers won in a period.
marketing_digital.media-planning: Deciding where, when and how often to run advertising to reach the target audience within a budget.
marketing_digital.sem: Search engine marketing: buying ads on search engines, usually paid per click, to appear for chosen keywords.
marketing_digital.retargeting: Showing ads to people who have already visited a website or used an app, to bring them back to convert.
marketing_digital.media-buying: Purchasing advertising space or time and negotiating prices and placements, following a media plan.
marketing_digital.programmatic-advertising: Buying digital ads automatically through software and real-time auctions, targeted at audiences rather than individual websites.
marketing_digital.salesforce-marketing-cloud: Salesforce's marketing platform for email, mobile messaging, customer journeys and audience data.
marketing_digital.marketing-attribution: Working out which marketing touchpoints and channels deserve credit for a conversion or sale.
marketing_digital.affiliate-marketing: Paying partners a commission for sales or leads they refer through their own sites or channels.
marketing_digital.ga4: Google Analytics 4, the current version of Google Analytics, which measures websites and apps through events.
marketing_digital.conversion-rate-optimization: Improving the share of visitors who take a desired action, such as signing up or buying, through testing changes to pages and journeys.
marketing_digital.semrush: An SEO and online visibility platform for keyword research, competitor analysis, site audits and rank tracking.
marketing_digital.landing-page-tests: Experiments that compare versions of a landing page to find which converts more visitors.
marketing_digital.google-analytics-4: The current version of Google Analytics, which measures website and app activity through events and reports on users and conversions.
marketing_digital.ahrefs: An SEO tool for analysing backlinks, keywords, competitors and site health.
marketing_digital.pardot: Salesforce's business-to-business marketing automation tool, now called Marketing Cloud Account Engagement, for email, lead scoring and nurturing.
marketing_digital.display-advertising: Visual ads, such as banners and rich media, shown on websites and apps through ad networks.
marketing_digital.on-page-seo: Optimising the content and HTML of individual pages, such as titles, headings and internal links, so they rank better in search.
marketing_digital.conversion-optimisation: Improving the share of visitors or users who complete a desired action, by testing changes to pages, offers and journeys.
marketing_digital.moz: An SEO software provider offering tools for keyword research, link analysis, rank tracking and site audits.
marketing_digital.screaming-frog: A desktop website crawler that SEO specialists use to audit sites for broken links, redirects, metadata and other technical issues.

product.cross-functional: Working across several teams or disciplines, such as engineering, design, sales and operations, toward a shared goal. Postings use it for roles that coordinate people they do not manage.
product.kpis: Key performance indicators: the few measures a team or business tracks to judge whether it is meeting its goals.
product.product-strategy: The plan that sets which problems a product will solve, for which customers, how it will win, and what the team will and will not build.
product.product-roadmap: A plan showing what a product team intends to build and roughly when, linked to goals and shared with the business.
product.product-vision: A statement of the long-term future a product aims to create for its users, which guides the strategy and roadmap.
product.product-lifecycle: The stages a product passes through, from idea and launch through growth and maturity to decline or retirement.
product.linear: An issue-tracking and project-planning tool used by software and product teams to manage tasks, sprints and roadmaps.
product.okrs: Objectives and key results: a goal-setting method in which each objective is paired with a few measurable results that show whether it was achieved.
product.sprint-planning: The meeting at the start of an agile sprint where the team chooses and commits to the work it will complete in that sprint.
product.customer-discovery: Interviewing and observing potential customers to understand their problems and test whether a product idea meets a real need.
product.mixpanel: A product analytics tool that tracks how users interact with an app or website through events, funnels and retention reports.
product.amplitude: A product analytics platform for measuring user behaviour, funnels, retention and experiments.
product.prioritisation: Deciding which work to do first by weighing value, cost, urgency and risk, often with a scoring framework.
product.feature-definition: Describing what a product feature must do and why, including the user problem, requirements and acceptance criteria, before it is built.
product.productboard: A product management tool for collecting customer feedback, prioritising features and sharing roadmaps.
product.roadmunk: A tool for building and sharing product roadmaps in timeline and swimlane views.

workplace_tools.excel: Microsoft Excel, the spreadsheet program used to organise, calculate and analyse data with formulas, pivot tables and charts.
workplace_tools.microsoft-office: Microsoft's suite of desktop and cloud productivity applications, including Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams.
workplace_tools.powerpoint: Microsoft PowerPoint, the program used to build slide presentations.
workplace_tools.jira: Atlassian's issue and project tracking tool, used to plan, assign and follow work such as tasks, bugs and sprints.
workplace_tools.slack: A team messaging app organised into channels, with direct messages, file sharing and integrations with other tools.
workplace_tools.notion: A workspace app combining documents, wikis, databases and task boards that teams use for notes and planning.
workplace_tools.confluence: Atlassian's team wiki for writing, organising and sharing documentation, meeting notes and project pages.
workplace_tools.sharepoint: Microsoft's platform for intranet sites, document storage and collaboration within an organisation.
workplace_tools.miro: An online whiteboard for collaborative diagrams, workshops, brainstorming and planning.
